gap: No result ChatGPT got states that XTAR's 1.5 V AA cells have their own charge-management chip and take 4.75–5.5 V only from a charger that supports XTAR's 1.5 V Li-ion protocol. That means a NiMH charger won't do it, and XTAR's own store says its VX4 V1 charger cannot charge the CLR 4300 that ChatGPT made its top pick.
standout_why: Charge-test (cited) lists 'MX4, L4 Pro, VX4, L4 and L8' as compatible chargers for the CLR 4300 and says to use 'a charger explicitly compatible' with the cells. It gives no VX4 version caveat and doesn't explain why other chargers fail. Light And Matter (cited) says a NiMH charger 'won't work' with the EBL cells, but it doesn't explain why and doesn't cover XTAR. Light And Matter also covers the EBL cells' sudden full-to-empty cutoff, and Charge-test covers the CLR 4300's sloped tail, so the low-battery-warning part of this mechanism is already partly covered. Digital Camera World returned only its title to my fetch, so I could not check its text. ChatGPT's own answer says only 'Requires a compatible charger' and doesn't name which chargers work.
decides: This confirms the XTAR CLR 4300 as the pick only if it's bought with a charger XTAR lists as compatible: the L4 Pro, MX4, L4 or L8, or a VX4 V2 but not a V1. The cheapest sure route is XTAR's USA L4 Pro + 4× CLR 4300 bundle at $39.99, against $26.99 for the batteries alone. Someone who already owns a NiMH charger, such as the Tenergy TN480U that Dealectric lists, can't charge these cells with it. The same mechanism explains each candidate's low-battery behaviour: the EBL holds 1.5 V and then cuts off, the XTAR 4150 steps down to 1.1 V, and the CLR 4300 declines linearly to about 1.0 V. In devices that judge charge by voltage, only the stepped and sloped designs give a warning before the device dies.

findings.label: Why ordinary chargers fail
findings.value: Charge-management IC is inside each cell; the cells 'must use chargers that support the 1.5V Li-ion protocol'; NiMH chargers may fail to charge or under-charge them
findings.note: XTAR's own page. It also says that in third-party tests with the LR 3000, the Vapcell BL4 and Soshine chargers worked and a Liitokala charger did not recognise the cell.

findings.label: Charging input (maker spec)
findings.value: 4.75–5.5 V at 0.45 ± 0.05 A; about 2.6 h with a dedicated 1.5 V AA charger
findings.note: The charger supplies about 5 V and the regulator inside the cell does the charging. A NiMH charger ends its charge around 1.4–1.5 V per cell, so it can't feed this input. That last point is my inference from the maker's spec.

findings.label: Max continuous discharge current
findings.note: XTAR's test-results page says Sven Greiner measured a 3.6 A burst before the protection tripped.

findings.label: Recommended chargers (maker spec)
findings.value: L4 Pro, MX4, L4, L8 (one version of the page also lists VX4)
findings.note: The VX4 listing is inconsistent across versions of the page. The store's V1/V2 notice settles it.

findings.label: Low-battery behaviour by discharge-curve class
findings.value: CV: holds 1.5 V then cuts off suddenly, no warning. CSR: holds 1.5 V then steps down to 1.1 V (XTAR AA 4150). CLR: holds 1.5 V then falls linearly to 1.0 V (XTAR CLR 4300, about 1.05 V near empty). LR: falls linearly from 1.5 V to 1.0 V (XTAR LR 3000)
findings.note: XTAR uses akkutests.de's classification. Its stated reason for the slope is that it 'allows compatible devices to detect the falling voltage and provide a low-battery indication before shutdown.'

findings.label: Regulator behaviour near empty (reviewer)
findings.value: Constant 1.5 V until empty; the device's battery gauge drops from full to empty at once
findings.source_title: Review: EBL Rechargeable 3000mWh AA Lithium-Ion Batteries – Light And Matter
findings.note: The reviewer saw this in a Nikon N90s and a Pentax 645. In a Godox TT685 flash at full power, recycle time was 10.72–17.55 s, against 2.23 s for the best NiMH, because overheating protection throttled the cells. This is a cited rival, so it is not new.
